pr_title: 3.0.0-alpha6: "openssl pkcs12" is unable to parse or create PKCS#12 archives with default ciphers
pr_body:
This PR makes the following two changes in openssl-pkcs12 to fix #11672 :

1. Changes the default encryption algorithms for certificates and private keys from RC2 to AES_256_CBC in OpenSSL 3.0
2. Add a new option "-legacy" to the pkcs12 cli which loads the legacy provider and restores the default algorithms
    The default algorithm for private key encryption is 3DES_CBC. If the legacy option is not specified, then 
     the legacy provider is not loaded and the default encryption algorithm for both certificates and private keys is
    AES_256_CBC by default.

The above design was proposed by @t8m as per the comments in the discussion #11672 that were agreed upon.

Documentation and example section is updated.
No new tests are added. The cli usage is documented under examples.

Usage:

openssl pkcs12 -in cert.pem -inkey key.pem -out foo.p12 -export
openssl pkcs12 -info -in foo.p12

with the legacy option:

openssl pkcs12 -in cert.pem -inkey key.pem -out foo.p12 -export **-legacy**
openssl pkcs12 -info -in foo.p12 **-legacy**

Note: certs and keys can be generated using the below command
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365

Hmmm, should this become a standard option alongside `-provider` and `-provider_path`?  I can't really see how it's justifiable to special case the "pkcs12" command...
Do we have clear use cases for this option with other commands? Or do you mean the generalized case to be "just load the legacy and default provider"?

The special case here is that we clearly need to change the defaults to something more modern with pkcs12 but the old defaults might be needed for interoperability AND they require the legacy provider. With other commands I do not see urgent need to change the defaults but if you think about any, where it makes sense, I'd agree with the generalization.

issue_context.title: 3.0.0-alpha1: "openssl pkcs12" is unable to parse or create PKCS#12 archives with default ciphers
issue_context.body:
Works in 1.1.1:
```
$ openssl version
OpenSSL 1.1.1d FIPS  10 Sep 2019
$ openssl pkcs12 -in cert.pem -inkey key.pem -out foo.p12 -export
Enter Export Password:
Verifying - Enter Export Password:
```

Fails in 3.0.0:
```
$ $HOME/openssl-3.0.0/bin/openssl version
OpenSSL 3.0.0-alpha1 23 Apr 2020 (Library: OpenSSL 3.0.0-alpha1 23 Apr 2020)
$ $HOME/openssl-3.0.0/bin/openssl pkcs12 -in cert.pem -inkey key.pem -out foo.p12 -export
Enter Export Password:
Verifying - Enter Export Password:
40:A7:D6:79:1B:7F:00:00:error:digital envelope routines:evp_generic_fetch:fetch failed:crypto/evp/evp_fetch.c:307:Default library context, Algorithm (RC2-40-CBC), Properties ()
40:A7:D6:79:1B:7F:00:00:error:digital envelope routines:EVP_CipherInit_ex:initialization error:crypto/evp/evp_enc.c:336:
40:A7:D6:79:1B:7F:00:00:error:digital envelope routines:EVP_PBE_CipherInit:keygen failure:crypto/evp/evp_pbe.c:132:
40:A7:D6:79:1B:7F:00:00:error:PKCS12 routines:PKCS12_pbe_crypt:pkcs12 algor cipherinit error:crypto/pkcs12/p12_decr.c:36:
40:A7:D6:79:1B:7F:00:00:error:PKCS12 routines:PKCS12_item_i2d_encrypt:encrypt error:crypto/pkcs12/p12_decr.c:133:
40:A7:D6:79:1B:7F:00:00:error:PKCS12 routines:PKCS12_pack_p7encdata:encrypt error:crypto/pkcs12/p12_add.c:119:
```
comments:
Adding "-provider legacy" to the command line should work around this.

I'm not sure about using RC2.

> I'm not sure about using RC2.

Unfortunately, is glaringly present in the RFC: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7292#appendix-C

Is this only the case where a password is used? Perhaps we should fail with a helpful error message if the right cipher is not available and tell the user to explicitly load the legacy provider? Or alternatively should we automatically load it?

There was a vote to not load the legacy provider by default, that's not ideal.

How would we warn the user when an algorithm isn't found?  The core fetch doesn't know that _RC2_ is a legacy algorithm.  It also doesn't know which provider _foobar_ comes from.

> How would we warn the user when an algorithm isn't found? The core fetch doesn't know that RC2 is a legacy algorithm. It also doesn't know which provider foobar comes from.

But we know that PKCS12 has a hard-wired dependency on RC2-40-CBC - and we know that specific cipher is in the legacy provider. So we simply try to fetch that before doing anything with PKCS12 and if we get `NULL` back then we display a nice error message to the user suggesting they add `-provider legacy`
So what you're saying, @mattcaswell, is that the `openssl pkcs12` commant should load the legacy provider as a fallback?  Or should we make that globally in the `openssl` app?
Internally, we can load but not activate a provider, and flag it as fallback.  It would be perfectly possible to add a public function for this, and have that be used by our application.

> So what you're saying, @mattcaswell, is that the openssl pkcs12 commant should load the legacy provider as a fallback? Or should we make that globally in the openssl app?

Well I suggested 2 possible paths:

1) Don't load legacy, but attempt to detect that we're failing because of an unavailable cipher and display a hint to the user that they might like to explicitly load the provider

or

2) Automatically load the legacy provider *for this one use case*

I do not think we should load it globally in the openssl app. The more I think about it the more I prefer (1) and the less I prefer (2). Although it might be tricky to get the detection right. Looking at the RFC there are a number of OIDs defined - some of which are in the legacy provider and some of which are not.

> Internally, we can load but not activate a provider, and flag it as fallback.

It would be just as easy to load the legacy provider.  Easier since the API already exists.


> Don't load legacy, but attempt to detect that we're failing because of an unavailable cipher and display a hint to the user that they might like to explicitly load the provider

This would be my preference.  What about printing a message along the lines of: _algorithm not found, does a provider need to be loaded?_
(Note I blocked user qa8302....they have been commenting on various issues/PRs with random spam)

> It would be just as easy to load the legacy provider. Easier since the API already exists.

... except someone might use a config file, and thereby define a whole different set of providers, in which case the legacy provider *should not* get activated.  That's why fallbacks exist in the first place.

> This would be my preference. What about printing a message along the lines of: algorithm not found, does a provider need to be loaded?

This is also my preference. How will we know that the error is caused by a missing algorithm?

I don't think we should over engineer things in the apps.  Talk of advanced detection gives me the heeby-geebies.  If you want to go down the route of advising the user, it should probably be done in a generic way, i.e. "This happened, you might want to add a different provider, for example '-provider legacy'"

> I don't think we should over engineer things in the apps. Talk of advanced detection gives me the heeby-geebies. If you want to go down the route of advising the user, it should probably be done in a generic way, i.e. "This happened, you might want to add a different provider, for example '-provider legacy'"

I'd be ok with that...but do we just do that for any error then? Or do we narrow it down somewhat?

> ...but do we just do that for any error then? Or do we narrow it down somewhat?

That depends on where the error is detected, doesn't it?  I.e. for function calls that is likely to call a fetch function down the callstack, we can choose to do this.  In case of uncertainty, do it for all.

> That depends on where the error is detected, doesn't it? I.e. for function calls that is likely to call a fetch function down the callstack, we can choose to do this. In case of uncertainty, do it for all.

Works for me - but we should probably make sure we have decent documentation about this for the pkcs12 app.

> Works for me - but we should probably make sure we have decent documentation about this for the pkcs12 app.

Agreed (what about other apps?)

> Agreed (what about other apps?)

Other apps probably need to be handled on a case-by-case basis.
But why not default to PBES2 with PBKDF2 algos? And perhaps add a -legacy option to create a legacy-encrypted pkcs12 which would also load the legacy provider?
What is the point of creating insecurely encrypted pkcs12 files by default in openssl-3.0?

> And perhaps add a -legacy option ...

This seems like a sensible suggestion.

The app framework could process the option and have it load the legacy provider _and_ set a global flag to enable other legacy behaviours.  It could be wrapped into the `OPT_PROV_OPTIONS` macro.
Perhaps reconsider the decision to not load the legacy provider.

> Perhaps reconsider the decision to not load the legacy provider.

No, please, we should not use RC2 and similar abominations **by default**. And not having legacy provider loaded  by default prevents this nicely.
Sure, not using weak crypto by default is a good thing.  So is not breaking existing applications. So is not breaking interop with external things.  It's all about trade-offs.

> And perhaps add a -legacy option ...

So there would be two ways to get the legacy providers loaded?

> But why not default to PBES2 with PBKDF2 algos?

Excellent thought!  PR welcome!  :wink:

> Sure, not using weak crypto by default is a good thing. So is not breaking existing applications. So is not breaking interop with external things. It's all about trade-offs.

I would never suggest something like this for 1.1.1 branch but I think it is very much appropriate and acceptable for 3.0 to change defaults. Because otherwise that would mean they are set-in-stone forever. We would not be taking away the possibility to create weakly encrypted things for interop with legacy systems completely. Just by default we would try to DTRT.
I'll work on the PR soon.

> But why not default to PBES2 with PBKDF2 algos?

This would be ideal.

> I'll work on the PR soon.

Awesome!

> So there would be two ways to get the legacy providers loaded?

There are two already :)  I'd see the `-legacy` option as doing more than just loading the provider.  It could change the defaults as well e.g.
What defaults?

With the `-legacy` option we could switch the defaults to the current ones as of 1.1.1 which provide maximum interoperability in expense of security :D Although the RC2 is used only for encrypting the certificate, so that is actually not really protecting much. 3DES is used for protecting the key but with a weak password key derivation function.

> But why not default to PBES2 with PBKDF2 algos?

You might want to be careful with this kind of thing. The default may have been part of a standard also. Also ask 'if I change this -will it break existing apps'.

But I think OpenSSL-3.0 can break interoperability with legacy software. That is something expectable with a major version update. Otherwise we would never be able to update to more up-to-date defaults ever.
